title: Strings
intro: Rust has two string types. `String` owns its text and can grow. `&str` is a borrowed, read-only view into text that lives somewhere else.

coming_from.go: `&str` looks like your `string`: read-only UTF-8 bytes, and `len()` counts bytes. The difference is lifetime. A Go substring shares its parent's bytes and the GC keeps the parent alive; a `&str` borrows from a `String` and can't outlive it, which the compiler checks. Slicing that cuts a rune gives Go invalid UTF-8 silently, while Rust panics. `range` gives (byte index, rune), which is `char_indices()`, not `chars()`.
coming_from.kotlin: Rust's `String` owns its text like a Kotlin `String`, but it can change, like a `StringBuilder`. `&str` has no Kotlin twin: it is a borrowed view into someone else's text, with no copy, and it can't outlive the string it points into. Rust stores UTF-8, not UTF-16, so `.len()` counts bytes and `.chars().count()` counts characters.
coming_from.python: Your `str` splits into two types: `String` owns text and can grow, `&str` is a borrowed view. Both are UTF-8 bytes, so `.len()` counts bytes, and slicing like `&s[0..1]` uses byte positions and panics if it cuts a character in half.
coming_from.typescript: JS strings are UTF-16, but Rust strings are UTF-8, so `.len()` counts bytes and `.chars()` walks characters like `for...of`. A `String` can also be changed in place with `push_str` when it's `mut`, and `&str` is a borrowed view of one.
coming_from.java: Rust's `String` owns its text like a Java `String`, but can grow like a `StringBuilder`. `&str` is a borrowed, read-only view into text with no copy, and it can't outlive the string it points into. Rust text is UTF-8, so `len()` counts bytes, and `s[1]` won't compile; use `chars()` to walk characters.
coming_from.csharp: `String` is an owned, growable string (think `StringBuilder`), and `&str` is close to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`: a borrowed view that can't outlive its owner. Rust stores UTF-8, not UTF-16, so `len()` counts bytes, and indexing with `s[1]` is not allowed.
coming_from.c: `String` is a heap buffer that frees itself, and `&str` is a pointer plus a length, like your `%.*s` view. Rust strings are always valid UTF-8, carry their length instead of a `'\0'`, and can't be indexed by byte with `s[1]`.
coming_from.cpp: `String` is like `std::string` and `&str` like `std::string_view`. But `std::string` holds any bytes, while Rust guarantees valid UTF-8. Rust also refuses `s[1]`, and the borrow checker stops a `&str` from outliving the `String` it views.

notes: Rule of thumb: a function that only reads text takes `&str`. A struct field that keeps text uses `String`.
A `&String` turns into a `&str` automatically when you pass it, so `fn f(s: &str)` accepts both.
`.len()` counts bytes, not characters. `é` takes 2 bytes, so "héllo" is 6 bytes and 5 characters.
Text written in quotes, like `"hi"`, is already a `&str`. Use `String::from("hi")` or `"hi".to_string()` when you need an owned String.

gotcha.title: Indexing a string like an array
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `s[1]` gives you a byte. For plain English text, that byte is the second letter, so it looks like it works.
gotcha.rust_sees: Rust stores text as UTF-8, where one character can be 1 to 4 bytes. Byte 1 of "héllo" is the first half of `é`.
gotcha.why: `s[1]` could mean byte 1 (half of `é`) or character 1. Look at the outputs: the same line gives a raw byte in some languages (Go, C, C++) and a character or UTF-16 unit in others (Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript). Rust won't guess which you meant. Ask for characters with `.chars()`, or raw bytes with `.as_bytes()`.

go.says: Go runs this and prints 195. `s[1]` is a single byte, the first half of `é`, not a character.
go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := "héllo"
	second := s[1]
	fmt.Println(second)
}

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints é. Kotlin indexes UTF-16 units, and `é` is one unit, so you get the whole character.

python.says: Python prints é. A Python str is indexed by characters (code points), not bytes, so `s[1]` gives a whole character.

typescript.says: Prints é. `s[1]` picks a UTF-16 unit, and `é` fits in one, so it is a whole character here.

java.says: `charAt(1)` gives `é` here because Java strings are made of UTF-16 units, and `é` fits in one.

csharp.says: C# strings are indexed by UTF-16 `char`, not by byte, and `é` fits in one, so `s[1]` is é.

c.says: C indexes bytes, and `s[1]` is the first of the two bytes in é. Whether `char` is signed depends on the platform. These outputs come from Linux on ARM64, where it is unsigned, so this prints 195. On x86 and on Apple-silicon Macs it is signed, and the same program prints -61. Either way you get a byte, not é.

cpp.says: `s[1]` is the first byte of the two-byte `é`. These outputs come from Linux on ARM64, where `char` is unsigned, so this prints 195 like Go. On x86 and on Apple-silicon Macs `char` is signed, and the same program prints -61. Either way you get a byte, not é.

owned = "héllo"  # str is a sequence of characters, and immutable
view = owned[0:1]  # slicing makes a new string

s = "go"
s += " + rust"  # builds a new string

print(f"{owned} {view} {s}")
print(f"bytes={len(owned.encode())} chars={len(owned)}")
for c in owned:
    print(f"[{c}]", end="")
print()
